paragraphs.text: Familial adult myoclonic epilepsy-2 (FAME2) is an autosomal dominant disorder with a core triad of cortical tremor, multifocal myoclonus, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures (Crompton et al., 2012). Cortical myoclonic tremor usually starts in the second decade of life, followed by overt myoclonic or generalized tonic-clonic seizures (Corbett et al., 2019). The course is nonprogressive (Guerrini et al., 2001). Expressivity varies within and between families, and the frequency of generalized tonic-clonic seizures ranges widely between families (Corbett et al., 2019).

They considered it a new epilepsy syndrome because its phenotype differed from that of familial adult myoclonic epilepsy and because it did not map to chromosome 8q23.3-q24. De Falco et al. paragraphs.text: Guerrini et al. (2001) described a pedigree with 8 affected individuals who had a nonprogressive disorder starting between the ages of 12 and 50 years. All patients had predominantly distal, semicontinuous rhythmic myoclonus and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and 3 had complex partial seizures. Most patients rarely had seizures and had normal cognition, but 3 with intractable seizures had mild mental retardation. All patients had frontotemporal and generalized interictal EEG abnormalities. Neurophysiologic study suggested that the myoclonus was of cortical origin. EEG activity over the contralateral rolandic area was coherent with EMG activity at 8 to 25 Hz and preceded it by 8 to 15 ms. The C-reflex at rest was enhanced, and somatosensory and visual evoked potentials were of high amplitude. Compared with controls, the resting motor threshold to transcranial magnetic stimulation was reduced and the post-motor evoked potential silent period was shortened. The authors concluded that these findings indicated diffuse cortical hyperexcitability.

paragraphs.text: Striano et al. (2005) reported a 5-generation family from Naples, Italy, with cortical tremor, myoclonus, and epilepsy. Eleven members, aged 24 to 56 years (mean, 39.2 years), had hand tremor and myoclonus, and 6 of them had generalized seizures. Electrophysiologic study showed cortical reflex myoclonus in all affected members. Three presymptomatic members had giant somatosensory evoked potential components and an enhanced long-loop reflex I. These 3 developed hand tremor and myoclonus of the upper limbs after 1.5 years of follow-up.

paragraphs.text: Suppa et al. (2009) studied an Italian family with familial cortical myoclonic tremor with epilepsy. Affected members had limb and voice tremor, seizures, and myoclonus of the eyelids during blinking. Neuropsychologic testing showed visuospatial impairment, possibly due to temporal lobe dysfunction. paragraphs.text: Crompton et al. (2012) reported a 6-generation kindred of European descent from New Zealand and Australia with 55 affected members. All had fine hand tremor, which typically began in adolescence (median age, 15 years; range, 4-60 years). Proximal myoclonus was present in 44 of 55 (80%) and started later than the hand tremor (median age, 17 years; range, 5-60 years). Generalized tonic-clonic seizures occurred in 8 of 55 (15%), with a median age at onset of 43.5 years (range, 18-76 years). These seizures occurred around sleep onset after severe generalized myoclonus. Neurophysiologic testing confirmed cortical reflex myoclonus. The most common phenotype in this family was a mild postural hand tremor resembling essential tremor, combined with subtle proximal myoclonus.

paragraphs.text: De Fusco et al. (2014) described a second Tuscan family with ADCME (family B), a 4-generation kindred with 5 affected members. All had postural myoclonus of the hands and upper limbs. Cortical tremor was the presenting symptom in every case and began between 18 and 50 years of age. All but 1 had epilepsy, with rare generalized tonic-clonic seizures that were sometimes precipitated by visual stimuli. Two patients also had drug-resistant focal motor or complex partial seizures. One patient had borderline cognitive level. Generalized or focal paroxysmal EEG activity was found in all patients. Jerk-locked back-averaged EEG, somatosensory evoked potentials, and long-loop reflexes were consistent with cortical reflex myoclonus. Two of the oldest mutation carriers developed age-related dementia. De Fusco et al. (2014) noted that the myoclonus often worsened in advanced age.

paragraphs.text: De Fusco et al. (2014) studied 2 Tuscan families with ADCME, including the family reported by Guerrini et al. (2001). They found a heterozygous in-frame insertion/deletion in the ADRA2B gene (c.675_686delTGGTGGGGCTTTinsGTTTGGCAG) that replaces 5 amino acids (HGGAL) with 4 new residues (QFGR) in the third intracellular loop. The variant was found by sequencing candidate genes in the critical region. It cosegregated with the disease and was absent from 575 Tuscan controls, dbSNP, the Exome Variant Server, and the 1000 Genomes Project. Targeted capture and next-generation sequencing of the critical region in 2 affected members of the first family found no other relevant variant. The 2 families shared the disease haplotype across the entire critical region. In transfected cells, the mutant receptor localized normally to the plasma membrane and was internalized normally in an arrestin-3-dependent manner. However, it did not form a stable complex with spinophilin after 10 minutes of epinephrine stimulation. In Xenopus oocytes, spinophilin increased the EC50 for epinephrine with the wildtype receptor but not with the mutant receptor. The authors concluded that the mutation had a gain-of-function effect and increased epinephrine-stimulated calcium signaling. They found no ADRA2B mutations in BAFME pedigrees from southern Italy that mapped to the same locus.

paragraphs.text: Corbett et al. (2019) analyzed whole-genome sequencing data from affected members of 3 families with FAME2. In all of them they found an expanded ATTTT repeat with an inserted ATTTC repeat in intron 1 of the STARD7 gene. The ATTTC repeat was absent from whole-genome sequencing data of 69 controls. Using repeat-primed PCR, they detected the ATTTC expansion in all 137 affected individuals from 16 previously reported families with FAME2. Two of 24 tested family members without a FAME diagnosis also carried it; both were from younger generations and likely presymptomatic. Among 72 additional individuals with clinical features similar to FAME, the expansion was found in 20 of 20 familial cases from 6 families and in 1 of 52 singleton cases. In total, the expansion segregated in 158 of 158 typically affected individuals from 22 pedigrees. It did not amplify in 28 unrelated control samples. Long-read sequencing in 1 patient showed 274 AAATG and 387 AAAAT repeats in one read and 345 AAATG and 390 AAAAT repeats in another, suggesting somatic variation in repeat size. A second patient had 588 AAATG and 340 AAAAT repeats, 4,645 bp in total. Corbett et al. (2019) also found the STARD7 expansion in the 2 families carrying the ADRA2B indel reported by De Fusco et al. (2014). They concluded that the ADRA2B allele was not causative.
